text_feedback.question: What are your three key learnings about your code-base from this session?
text_feedback.response:
Key take aways:
1. Testing the behaviour rather than unit of code i.e  Unit testing system rather than implementation
2. Testing pyramid is ultimate testing strategy - Focus should me more towards top of the pyramid. For example testing the functionality (group of classes)
3. Team should define tolerance level for code duplication - treating unit test on par with production code

Here’s what we discussed: 
1.	The data as we know: 
a.	The team has approximately 400 manual tests that get executed before a release, with a code-size of ~50k lines.
b.	Currently there are sanity tests that are executed before the build, but there are opportunities to improve.
c.	By Q1 2020, there are plans of migrating all the code-bases to TFS-GIT and CICD pipelines to TFS.
d.	An audit was conducted in the past, and recommendations came out that increasing the strengths of unit-tests and coverage would help.
e.	Developers run Resharper for static code analysis at their desk, and this is on a “best effort” basis, and is not gated. 
f.	Some new projects are getting initiated and/or some projects are still in its early stages, and the team is looking at ways of upholding code-quality via gating in such projects.
2.	The recommendations:
a.	We start with test duplication detection by running cosine-similarity tool with the team. This will ensure that if there are duplicates in manual tests, the problem of time-to-market can be reduced immediately and with minimal involvement of the team or disruption to schedule.
b.	We start integrating smart-test ordering that’ll look at connects between git-commits and test-files and tell us what tests have to be run in what order based on the commits made to the code base, there-by helping in identifying what tests to run to check sanity.
c.	We’ll target unit-test coverage for some common patterns, and how we can achieve them in the code. 
d.	We’ll also look at how we can introduce the right gates at developer box, at local builds and at common builds.
e.	We’ll also look at how we can strengthen the unit-tests asserts with mutation testing.
f.	With the above ones set in place, we can look at deduplication of the codebase.
3.	Next actions:
a.	Pattabhi and Brijesh: Setup a meeting with the team to on-board them to similarity analysis.
b.	Datta: Setup a meeting with the team to understand unit-tests gaps and how we can bridge them.
c.	Datta: Setup a meeting with the team on gating practices we can introduce in the code-base. 
d.	ICAP team: To ensure that no further degradation of code happens, via code-review policies on unit-test coverages.
e.	ICAP team: Start documenting root-cause analysis of identified defects and tie it down to code/test/build practices, and develop a continuous loop of learning & gating.
f.	ICAP Team: If the team finds value in the actions being taken, setup a 1-day-per-month rule on addressing such debts with 10% of their dev-team working with SWCoE to actively address debts (one day in a month).

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response: I was able to change the direction of content delivery from a topic specific training to a journey specific training, starting with defining the behavior of the use-case, then applying TDD, then mutation testing, then duplication detection, then static code analysis, then CICD.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
I suggested that, since the pair programming exercise is informal, it would be nice to capture the "break-throughs" done via pair programming, in a wiki page, so that it can be used at a later point of time to: 
1. Showcase the effectiveness of pair-programming. 
2. Identify opportunities which can be automated and made as a part of CICD pipeline so that everybody gets its benefits for free.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response: In the problem presented to us, JSCPD was ignoring one file in a folder of two files, and the team was not able to identify why. They mentioned that TICS identifies two files and measures duplicates, but JSCPD doesn't. I was able to quickly identify the issue with JSCPD. JSCPD defaults the size of a file to 30kb. Any file that's greater than 30kb is ignored. I gave them the solution of using the -z option to specify the maximum threshold of the file (-x 1000mb in this case) and they were able to run JSCPD successfully, and were able to identify more duplicates with a token count of 50.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response: We were able to quickly come up with a plan to adopt pair-programming experiment with HSDP-CP team in PIC-B. I will be leading this for the next two months. With a commitment of 1hr per day. We'll revisit the plan again in Feb-end 2020, to see if were are doing this good, or if we need to change course. The idea is to make teams self sufficient to run pair-programming on their own.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
We were able to kick-start the 6 months series of I-will-code! We identified the use-case (Calculator) and the first operation (addition). This exercise, as agreed by everyone will follow the same model of that proposed for Bootcamp for FTH's. We'll follow BDD, with mutation testing and all other concepts. 

The first session identified the behaviors of a calculator for an addition scenario. The next session targets writing behaviors identified, into a gherkin style format.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
We identified that there are 4 different programming languages in this project. Java, C#, R and Python. We can approach the "correct code @ desk" for each of these programming languages, one at a time. Given that Java was the most popular one (80% of the code base) we'll chose that first, and then C# and then python, and then R. 

In the workshop, we'll identify tools & techniques that'll help teams code better as and when they write code, and not wait till CICD to assert it. CICD, when its ready, will be used to assert the rules followed during development/coding.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
1. We were able to resolve the problem
2. We were able to identify low-hanging fruits and how to fix them. 
3. We were able to come up with a logical plan of handling low-hanging fruit & get to approximately 900 lines of reduced code in 20 mins. 
4. Get a commitment from the team that when they are ready to make the change, they'll send us the before, after, commitid and the source code link - so that we can create a record of the data. 
5. Adopt JSCPD into the OS team, where they can run duplication detection & similarity analysis on their batch-files. 


Appreciation: Sapna appreciated that even a layman like her can look at the report and make sense out of the data generated.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
We were able to identify an initial checklist - that can potentially be automated. We also identified why we'd need pair-programming, and how we'd keep track of the "wins" during the pair-programming. After every session, we'll collect anonymised data on what went went well, and what could have improved. This will help ensure that we keep track of the progress & value adds from each session of pair-programming.

The checklist identified includes: 
No checkstyle errors
Less code duplications
Proper exception handling
Input validation
Dispose pattern check
Test coverage & strengths of the unit-tests
Cyclometric complexity check
Synchronisation problem check
Performance degradation checks
Ensuring SOLID principles (SRP mainly)
Backward compatibility
Localization/Internationalization/Formatting
Logging checks - for performance & values
Argument counts
Visibility of a method!
Dependency injection, Mocking & test-coverages
Strong asserts vs weak asserts
Test decoupling
Mutation testing & data boundaries
Race-condition checks
Memoisation/short-term-in-memory cache
Ternary operator vs if-else statements
Timestamp normalization

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response: We were able to identify some of the data-points that Philips' research team looks at, for which they can leverage Cerberus, and continue towards making Cerberus an open-source code-base where folks can continue to contribute.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
We identified how to set goals that add business value to the organization. Here are things that we signed up to help the team out:
- Identifying how to specify code-quality goals in a pom.xml or a gradle’s build file. Show examples of how it can be done, adopt a few goals into a project and run the build. Show the goals that SWCoE follows currently for its implementation.
- Help facilitate (if necessary) discussion with TA team, on how to gate a build wrt previous build output (Can be applicable to unit-test results, integration test results, sanity test results etc.)
- Help in facilitating either templatizing or automating common code review comments, identified because a production issue was root-caused to this common code review comment.
- Any other help needed that ties back to a business outcome.

We also kept an open forum and perhaps set up a once-a-<frequency> meeting model instead of the 6th month and end-of-year engagement model. 

I volunteered to informally help the team with anything they need.

text_feedback.question: What was the value add?
text_feedback.response:
We identified that although the team is in its early stage of software development, we can still work on quality@desk tools. The way we'll pilot this is, explore one tool, adopt it in to the IDE, see the report, make changes to improve the quality, and then move on to the next tool. 

We start with sonarlint. Then hopefully move towards improving unit-test coverage, and then run mutation testing and other tools like duplication detection etc.

raw_data_sample.What was the value add?: In the problem presented to us, JSCPD was ignoring one file in a folder of two files, and the team was not able to identify why. They mentioned that TICS identifies two files and measures duplicates, but JSCPD doesn't. I was able to quickly identify the issue with JSCPD. JSCPD defaults the size of a file to 30kb. Any file that's greater than 30kb is ignored. I gave them the solution of using the -z option to specify the maximum threshold of the file (-x 1000mb in this case) and they were able to run JSCPD successfully, and were able to identify more duplicates with a token count of 50.

The Autopsy/NFF Pilot aims to dramatically improve the quality, completeness, and actionability of Service DEFOA autopsy outputs by:
	• Detecting repeated DEFOA cases automatically.
	• Identifying and escalating high‑risk NFF (No Failure Found) cases that may mask underlying failure patterns.
	• Strengthening supplier diagnostic quality and reducing recurring part failures.
	• Closing the loop faster between SPS, BU, Suppliers, and Markets.
This pilot directly addresses the gaps and opportunities documented in existing DEFOA materials, including:
	• Incomplete supplier autopsy reports (many missing or delayed).
	• Large backlog of ZREP/ZRFA parts pending root-cause analysis.
	• High NFF volume impacting corrective actions.
	• Inconsistent owner group assignment & case closure rules.
Lack of actionable analytics across suppliers and modalities.

text_feedback.question: For someone who is aspiring to improve their interviewing skills and is looking up to you, what technique(s) would you suggest to them, that you found very useful for yourself by being part of thi...
text_feedback.response:
• Preparation prior to the interview is paramount (review of the resume, Job Description, past round feedback, red flags)
• Evaluation needs to be structured and fact-based coupled with instincts
• Rapport building is key. As bar raisers, we have a short window to establish that through the course of the discussion. It is important to create a cordial atmosphere coupled with mutual respect to enable candid conversations.
• Start with the basics – invest time to understand if the candidate has clarity about the role based on past discussions with panelists. This is one of the important steps towards calibrating expectations and long term fit to Philips
• Different strokes for different folks: 
(i) A template definitely helps to guide the conversation. On the same token, it is important to tailor the discussion thread based on the candidate’s profile and how the interaction evolves.
(ii) It is important for the bar-raiser to effectively elicit from the candidate his / her ability to apply past / current experience to the role.
(iii) Key areas that I make it a point to explore are cultural fit, behaviors, maturity, dealing with ambiguity and strategic thinking
• Presenting role plays and scenarios provide important insights related to the value system of the candidate
• Debrief is critical. 
(i) It provides the opportunity for the bar-raiser to put forth key insights that could potentially enable the hiring manager to plan the candidate’s transition into the role and ramp-up in a smoother manner. 
(ii) It can also serve a forum to understand common observations that stand out and also if there are any surprises that are not red flags but need attention.
• As brand ambassadors for Philips, it is important for us to role model the Philips behaviors and above all ensure a memorable candidate experience.
